game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If there were a "maybe" option for recommending this game I would have given it that, but with only a "yes" or "no" choice unfortunately I have to just come down on the side of the latter.

This game is essentially a "choose your own adventure" detective novel wherein your decisions are all made by choosing which information to share with - or conceal from - the authorities. The concept is an interesting one and the game does throw up some nice surprises in both the gameplay and the plot, and there are occasional moments of humour.

However, the limitations in using conflicting information are rather annoying. For example sometimes the game will let you choose only one of two (or more) different pieces of information even when both are true and could be vital to successfully completing your objectives. (I get that this is a key game mechanic, but I think it could be explained or handled better to make the game feel less forced.) In particular there is one key decision which just comes down to a 50/50 guess with no supporting information to help the player make the correct choice. (I am talking about the part where the player must determine the third location - If I missed any clues as to which is the correct answer, somebody please tell me!)

Another major concern is the quality of the writing; whilst for the most part the writing is capable and there are some memorable moments, the writing is never compelling - I gave up reading about halfway through my first playthrough, instead just scanning text for the (conveniently highlighted) choices. Whilst I can forgive bad writing in some games, for a game that is all about the writing the standard really needs to be higher. Some of the text simply drags on too long, especially any form of dialogue (phone calls, chat text, etc.) - this is doubly annoying for dialogue as there is no way to skip it. (Usually you can just let it run in the background whilst you read other in-game documents, but be careful with this as some actions are time-critical.)

Replay value may depend how willing you are to work through the text again. Whilst it is nice to see the different outcomes your actions can have, it feels like 90% or more of the game remains identical so it becomes a slog to see the few changes or pick up achievements. Some of the achievements are so ambiguously described that the only way to complete them seems to be relying on lots of replays and blind luck, or of course walkthroughs.

It is a shame to see such a nice idea and plot wasted without sufficient polish, but if the devs learn from this I do look forward to seeing what else they can produce.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: I think Orwell as a game is a great concept, but could have been executed far better. The game highlights important information, and railroads you into making choices that aren't backed by evidence. It doesn't provide enough detail for you to make judgement calls, but leaves you between two equally plausible answers, and forces you to make a choice. A better way of doing this would have been to present more information than necessary, and let players sort out what's important, and take their own notes. I would have preferred the game to involve less bias - letting players make their own choices, and come to their own conclusion on the benefits - or invasions - of government surveillance. I also feel the ending was robbed from me. I simply couldn't figure out how to support the cause of Thought, and wanted to have to face the ethical dilemma of doing so. Instead, I had to give them in as the only way to move forward. I really wanted to like this game, but I ultimately can't recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game will have you be FBI in a world where the NSA collects and store [i]everything[/i] but doesn't share it with you.

First off I rarely do reviews here on Steam but this game deserves it. Not because it's inherently bad game design, I don't think it is so much. Not because I just personally didn't like it or anything like that. I actually enjoyed the design choices both in terms of gameplay and aesthetics, it just works as is, nothing great but nothing terrible either. I have to review this and end up not recommending it because it's not even close to anything worth being called "Orwell". It's just not Orwellian enough, not thought-provocative enough. If you want to experience something more Orwellian just sign up on Facebook right now if you don't already have an account. It's even [i]"free"[/i]!

This game is overall a good piece of interactive narrative that can get you thinking about the implications of indiscriminately sharing every last little tidbit surrounding your life, and how that which you choose to share, along with other information available out there about yourself, can and will be used to create an image of you that might not necessarily be the whole picture. It's also good social commentary on the whole deal surrounding what makes an actual terrorist in today's world; This is immediately apparent as protesters early in the game protesting against mass surveillance because, well, mass surveillance, are portrayed as "anti-governmental terrorists" without much more context to legitimize that label.

What [b]this game isn't[/b] however is[b] a game about mass surveillance[/b]. As this is the whole selling point of this game I can't really recommend it, no matter how I otherwise enjoyed the game - for what it actually is. It's almost to the point where I would consider this to be false advertisement. You're not Big Brother, not even close. You're the In-Between Brother, looking down on Little Brother, bossing him around; But in the end both you and Little Brother are in a complete chokehold by Big Brother - no match, not even close.

What I'm trying to say is that this game does a good job of portraying how [b]directed surveillance[/b], what could be considered actual legit surveillance techniques, can be used to make decisions on who to pin crimes on after the fact. The game specifically portrays collection of information from social media as self-publicized, along with information gathered in general around the whole internet about a person, as this information is available when [b]specifically being looked for[/b]. That last part make a world of a difference. If a social media post has been removed by a user in this Orwellian future, well guess what, Big Brother can't see that post either. Orwellian, isn't it? Provocative, isn't it? 

The game does make some thought-provocative points around this theme of directed surveillance and social media content and in general hits the spot on that. In this day and age however it just isn't Orwellian enough, as what we have in our society today in terms of actual massive surveillance capabilities far surpasses anything remotely portrayed in this game.

So in conclusion, if you happen to feel that Big Brother-urge grow in you and all you want is to see how you would conduct yourself on the other side of the fence looking down on the sheeple, well look elsewhere. This won't be your fix. If you on the other hand feel like doing some detective work in a social media/online context and occasionally pin crimes on innocents for those authoritarian kicks, this might be your fix after all!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'm stopping because of the mechanic: Conflicted Datachunks.

You're presented two conflicting stories and have to choose which is true.  It's fun when you can figure out why the stories conflict. Most of the time, though, there's not enough evidence.  And once you make a choice - there's no going back.

This is opposite of how we should handle conflictings ideas. It's important to avoid jumping to conclusions - something your counterpart Symes does consistently. It's important to be open to possibilities and revise your position if new valid evidence comes in.

We're all subject to confirmation bias - games can teach us how to recognize and manage it.  "Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments" is a better model for dealing with difficult, uncertain decisions.

I'm happy Osmotic Studios is tackling such weighty topics in their games, but it also means the skills the player practices need to build solid foundations for dealing with those issues.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Didn't work for me. Not as a game.
It was an okay-interesting story, but the game played itself. I never had to think, just drag some highlighted text from the right to the left. And when the game actually put me in a situation where I had to think, by giving me the choice between two hypotheses, it did so with too little information. It felt especially bad because the game is fake-real-time, meaning things happen "as time goes by", but really only the game progresses as you take actions. So what would almost always happen was that (literally) immediately after submitted your hypothesis - your guess - as a FACT, the game goes "oh, this just in! Here's the information you could have used to make a sound judgement, if you'd just waited to click send for 5 seconds!". You continuously felt like an absolute impatient amateur switching between doing monkey work gathering information and then posting your guesses as facts to a board. And why can't I then write them and say "Hey, I just got this information! You know that thing I said earlier? Yeah, something has come up, and that is now completely wrong!" Absolutely destroyed my immersion.
All in all, the game just made me more and more annoyed, as the focus was more on "gut-feeling" than "deduction" (and maybe there's some social commentary on that. I never got it). In the end, the game feels more like a visual novel with tacked on interactive elements - more than it feels like an immersive story where you feel like an Orwellian observer and manipulator.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought this game because of all the good reviews, and while the game was enticing at certain times, and it had a great premise; it's literally only 5 hours worth of gameplay and that's it. There isn't even a repetive mode like in Papers, Please where you can at least mess around in the game outside of the story. There's no sub-quests, or sub-stories. There's nothing but the very short main story and CREDITS "THANKS FOR PLAYING". The ending is very unrewarding as well.

If this game were a few bucks, I wouldn't have complained; but $10+ depending on when you bought it? I guess it's better than going to the movies (in some ways), but I was left very unfulfilled by this. If all 5 of those hours were gripping and suspenseful like the few moments in this game that were? It'd have been worth it, but it doesn't quite succeed at that.

TL;DR: Not a bad game, but only one storyline, no sub-plots, no game to be done outside of the main story. Main story is also waaaay too fast. Also not much diversity in storyline no matter what you choose/do. You are pretty much just walked through the entire storyline the whole game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TL;DR: Don't bother, you're basically just a human web-crawler.

This game completely misses the point of what Orwellian infrastructure would look like in the first place and does everything in its power to not allow you any information at all. This game has no right to call itself Orwell, it has nothing to do with surveillance. Yea you have access to data, but the constant opinionated non-rational commentary by the "Adviser" undermines the whole of it. I can't of course claim the outcome wouldn't be the same in an actually Orwellian policy, but it sure as hell shouldn't look like this. In no way am I defending Orwellian values either, but their implementation here is.. well it isn't. It's just not there.
When choose information to be considered, the information changes between the point where you drag it from and the actual information recorded. 
The UI is unintuitive and very hard to navigate. The artificial load times don't help either, from both the gameplay loop and story-telling perspective, they make no sense.

Just to blow of some steam about how disappointed I am in this game, I'll address a couple reviews:

“Grabs the problem of how we balance our own liberty and our safety and turns it into a thrilling adventure.” 9/10 – Polygon
It does make a feeble attempt at tackling the problem of balancing safety and liberty, but fails miserably. Not only does it not represent what you could call Orwellian infrastructure, it doesn't even try. Access to information is limited and the information itself misinterpreted. Your "superior" is clearly opinionated, easily influenced and not of very high deductive capacity. Hardly a "thrilling adventure", the pace of the game is dictated by the game, not by the player. You can't move fast, despite the game making constant remarks about how you should. Nothing about this is thrilling, it's a very slow burner, except it isn't good. It's attempting to show flaws in Orwellian policies but fails to represent them, only showing flaws in its own design.

“A harrowing look into a reality where Big Brother is always watching” Rock Paper Shotgun
The only "harrowing" thing about this game is how it managed to get out of indev. The UI of this game is atrocious in both mechanical as well as logical sense. Mechanically navigating anywhere in this game is a pain in the bum, and the game punishes you every time you try to make more than 1 action per 10 seconds. The whole bit about conflicting data chunks is just stupid. First of all it should have a dating mechanism in the data collection software, which would prevent 90% of the data chunk conflicts in the first place. Secondly, why bother trying to pick one out of the 2 conflicting data points when all you're doing is presenting to someone who can clearly barely tie their own shoe-laces, much less decide outcomes for other people. I wouldn't let this "Adviser" choose the color of desktop background, much less my or anyone else's legal standing. Oh and did I mention: You can't go back on whatever the "Adviser" was saying either, so tough luck if you wanted to submit 2 pieces of information and started navigating before you can notice the Adviser popping up on screen, immediately skipping possibly vital dialog.

“In an age where so much personal information is willingly released by so many, Orwell brilliantly explores the implications of this data being misinterpreted.” 8/10 – GameSpot
This. That's the exact problem with the game, there isn't supposed to be an interpretation to be done in the first place. At the start of the game, you're presented with the job of a data-gatherer. It's not up to you to interpret this data and neither should it be up to the "Adviser". Not just because his brain activity matches that of a fork, but because he simply does not have all the data. Neither does the player, nobody does. Once the information is conclusive all on it's own and only then should there be an attempt at interpretation. It's a simple rational analysis up until then. Or at least it should've been. Instead the game constantly pedals it's own point with forced story-telling.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
While the story is interesting and I can see replayability in knowing you've made the wrong move, then creating a new profile and trying to avoid that scenario... I haven't done that. I probably won't either, because I have to agree with other players: the game guides you too much.

You're basically told where to click and when, which completely defeats the point of having all of these fun tools at your disposal--they might as well have dumped all data pieces in a list and had you click on them one by one, all after the other.

The auto-highlighting spoils the point of reading anything. The game warns you that potential choices conflict instead of letting the player decide on how thoroughly they want to investigate before submitting information. Some pieces of info feel completely useless, but your supervisor somehow decides they have more value than they should and the supervisor's decision often feels like a complete whim. And vice-versa: bits of info you feel should be important are locked away or not even meant to be accessible because the game decided "Nope, I won't even let you go into that dead-end for fun".

I guess this was worth what I paid for it... $2! and no more. This had a lot of promise but it doesn't have enough depth or freedom of choice for my tastes.

review_text_raw:
Short and simple.
It has a very enjoyible narrative where you play as a sort of detective.
Gameplay is limited by rules that are stated in the begining. 

Some more information?
The game is designed for the curious and detective types to search through forums, profiles, live text channels, and police reports to figure out who and why the cause of horrible events happen.
However you can also just as effectively "play" the game by scrolling through the pages only looking for the light-blue highlighted words to which you click and drag to the left on the profiles. For live chat rooms, you can just wait for information to show up that is able to be clicked on. The only time where you make a true decision is if you find yellow-highlighted text that contridicts information located somewhere else.

As a narrative experience for those who want to relax back and feel part of the story, this game is fantastic for you.
 For those who thought this would be a Challenging experience will be dissatisfied by simplistic gameplay of clicking and dragging.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The short review: I enjoyed playing this game, but I wouldn't recommend it. You should give it a try and form your own opinion though!

The long review: The game frustrated me because I expected a lot more narrative-wise since they used the name "Orwell". It definitely had parts where it excelled. The art is fantastic. The evidence gathering mechanic is a fun take on the traditional point and click genre. The story maintains a sense of mystery and suspense that can hook you in for the most part. Trying to figure out who Goldfels is and whether or not their intentions are truly malicious was what drove me to keep playing. I loved that there were also little easter eggs, such as a reference to "giraffes in hats" and articles about a 50 shades ripoff movie that made the game world feel more alive.

However, the writing... that's where this game falls short. There are other reviews talking about how the dialogue could be better etc., and I agree with them, but it wasn't the worst thing ever and it didn't ruin my experience. What DID ruin things for me was the game's last chapter. The narrative took a nosedive and the payoff completely ruined the setup. Most other reviews had no issue with the ending though, so you should definitely reserve your judgement and play the game first!


*****Some spoilers ahead*****

Just for context, I've only played this game once, and in my playthrough I prevented the 3rd bomb from exploding and decided to turn in evidence against Catherine Delacroix at the end.

The thing I hated MOST about this last chapter was the twist. Basically, one of the characters go "I was the person behind all those bombings bwahahaha". A real Reiner Braun moment.

This twist ending had two effects. First, it completely undermined the established mystery. Immediately, I felt stupid for caring about the game at all. What was the point of me working so hard then? Why did I collect all that evidence, if the criminal was just going to out themselves like that? 

The second effect was it made the whole narrative thematically unsatisfying. In the ending I received (I don't know if there are other possibilities), the criminal become the leader of the activist group with no repercussions. This was a person who'd set up two bombs that killed people. What pissed me off the most was that this person's friends acknowledges that this person committed murder, but based on the ending, it suggests all of them had decided to look the other way. Apparently, murder and thought manipulation is not a big deal when THEY are the ones doing it. So am I supposed to sympathise with this irresponsible group of people who have showed no regard for human life?? It's feels extremely hypocritical.

It really frustrated me because this game keeps telling me these people are innocent and I'm ruining their lives, but these people clearly aren't innocent. The worst things they did included: killing a police officer, doxxing a government agent, bombing and killing people at two separate locations, then attempting to cover up their crimes. Granted, some of these characters are more justified in their actions, but that doesn't change the fact that they actively ruined or tried to ruin people's lives. The only person I can say is mostly harmless in all of this is Themba. The game could've easily made this more nuanced by adding just one completely innocent character for the player to falsely incriminate. This one change would've easily revealed the flaws of the Orwell surveillance system, but that's not what happened. Instead, the game tries to guilt-trip you into feeling bad for outing people who have ACTUALLY done terrible things.

Maybe I only had a bad experience because my choices sucked. Maybe there is an ending where I get a better experience and justice is served to all, but then that implies there is a "right" way to choose, therefore you SHOULDN'T have the freedom to choose, your thoughts should be RESTRICTED so you choose only what the game thinks is right.

So what exactly is this game trying to tell me?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
An amazing concept, but the result is disappointing.
1) You do not investigate. You search documents for highlighted clues that you may upload into an investigation database. And you cannot delete them when they turn out to be misleading. Naturally i was careful not to upload dubious claims. Wrong. That gets you stuck. Orwel thrives on rumours, you have to upload these to get new related documents.

2) The writing is boring. The rudimentary gameplay wouldn't matter if the writing was fresh, but the documents you have to go through are as boring as real corporate websites and random people's blogs. Add an annoying coworker and you start regretting you have got that job.

3) The game only pretends to tackle complex issues of privacy and security. The Government is a classical dystopian government that can and will prosecute on "suggestive evidence" which can easily be an off-hand remark of a third party taken out-of-context. If you do not like that, you can side with bomb-throwing anarchists. No third option though, so either way there will be bad outcomes. And that is why surveillance is bad, or so the logic goes.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wish there were a rating between recommended and not recommended. Like a 'Eh, maybe?' option.  This game is very well designed with a great UI and intuitive progression. You do make some decisions and those decisions do have a pretty big impact on the story, but that is also where the bulk of my criticism comes from.

The decisions that make a huge difference feel incredibly arbitrary, so instead of feeling like you're investigating and making decisions, it feels like a game of guessing what the *developers* want you to do. It also railroads you into things I don't agree with and wouldn't choose to do, but if you don't do them you get stuck or really bad things happen. The guy you interact with (your point of contact) is very volatile and makes weirdly intense decisions off of very limited information, which can entirely screw up your game if you're going for the best results for everyone involved and it can be really hard to tell when he's going to do that. 

Initially I tried to play cautiously, withholding information I felt could be abused, and that ended up with people dying. So I quit where I was and restarted the whole game (boring, because this game is not very replayable) and had to try a few times before I figured out exactly what was causing the issue. Then I thought I better understood the game so I continued, only to find that I gave *too much* information to them which resulted in more deaths. 

It just doesn't feel like a game where the goal is about making the *best* decisions, it feels like a game where the goal is making whatever decisions the devs want you to make, and that's too much random guesswork to be fun for me. I stopped playing after Chapter 2 because I was tired of trying to read their minds.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's really hard for me to determine whether I do or don't recommend this, as I'm right on the line. I think overall, though, I have to lean into not recommending it.

The game starts off really well, with a really balanced juxtaposition of people being concerned about privacy versus the very real result of what you're able to accomplish through spying, really highlighting the blurred line between privacy and security. Further, the fact that there are rules in place - such as you can't hack someone without what is essentially a warrant from higher up in the system - makes it feel more grounded, and honestly like a more fair system. 

However, as you reach the end of the game, this completely falls apart. In the closing act, you get beaten around the head with the game designers' opinion, which is a very black-and-white "spying bad, privacy good", which entirely undermines the nuance the entire game up until that point had executed so well. I'll save the spoiler-filled rant for the end.

In addition to this, the gameplay has some glaring flaws. There are certain pieces of information that you absolutely [i]must[/i] collect to move forward, which is sometimes information that seems completely irrelevant (and you're outright told not to submit irrelevant information), forcing you to comb through every possible source with a fine-toothed comb, and sometimes just guess what they want you to submit.

Also, you can only extract verbatim phrases to submit, devoid of any context or clarification. Often, this leads to bizarre interpretations from the game. Like, apparently the game makers think [spoiler]that Depression or PTSD are things that make someone dangerous, rather than being a potentially debilitating disability[/spoiler]. Or perhaps you want to flag one piece of information because of it's context, but because that context isn't part of the auto-selected snippet, the game completely misinterprets it. For example, [spoiler]one girl is in a relationship with a guy, and helps herself to his wallet to make a couple purchases. Any reasonable person would have enough context to say, "Oh, she's borrowing his wallet, and he's only mildly annoyed that she's spending a lot? Clearly they are in a very serious relationship." game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: While the concept of the game is interesting I think it's not executed very well. Often times the game gets into a state where you can't collect any more information and you need to provide the surveillance system with data that you found. But there would often be two conflicting datasets, usually diametrically opposite, available for upload but you have no real way of determining which one is true/false. So you end up just taking the best guess and then the game starts playing this dramatic music because it's exactly at that point that somebody has to suddenly make a phone call or send an email with some sort of a revelation. Needless to say most of the time it doesn't land for me. My reaction to these situations would mostly be: "Oh, ok. I guess that's what happened.". The game goes out of its way to put you in a dead-end situation that could go either way and then it tries to make a tense situation out of it. It doesn't really work for me and I felt like the writing wasn't very strong in general. Especially when it comes to one character that communicates directly with you and beats you over the head with expository information and game tips in a way that attempts to be subtle but isn't really.

I really had high hopes for this game, you know? Unfortunately, it didn't quite hit the mark for me. The pace felt a bit sluggish, like waiting for water to boil. And the user interface? Well, let's just say it took a bit of getting used to – kind of like figuring out a new gadget.

Then there's this thing with the HQ, where you're left second-guessing whether they'll appreciate your findings or not. It's like trying to read someone's mind without the manual.

Now, don't get me wrong, if you're into diving deep into lore and soaking up every detail, this game might be right up your alley. But for someone like me, who prefers a bit more action-packed gameplay, it didn't quite scratch the itch.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I played this game through once, and am surprised to read so many positive reviews, especially about the witing and characterisation which was weak, cliched and overall, spoilt my sense of immersion. 


I felt railroaded by this game- especially by your "advisor" who is constantly interrupting with inane nonsense. I rarely felt as though my choices seemed to matter. More so at the end, but by then I'd already resigned myself to the fact that this was an experience, not a game. 


The story itself was fine, and I like the general idea and premise of the game- putting you in the role of the investigator, making decisions which would cause the lives or deaths of the people you were investigating in, what must be seen as, a morally dubious way. 

The problem is, I never really did feel as though I was investigating, because for at least the first two days the game completely spoon feeds you, and feels as though nothing you do matters- the course of the story is inevitable. I don't mind being railroaded, but the game should at least have the illusion of choice. Every "data chunk" you upload causes something else to beep, leading you to the next. There is very little true decision making till the last day. 

Another problem is the extremely weak cast of characters who are all based on familiar and unimaginative stereotypes: the rebellious rich girl, the arrogant rockboy agintant, the foriegn professor with a mysterious past. The stereotypes might have been passable if it were not for the atociously written dialogue, which felt more like a high school drama conducted entiely by people with sub-par IQs. I found myself disliking all the characters and being irritated by the dialogue which so clearly served an agenda to ilucidate parts of the plot, instead of giving any sense of them being real people with real motivations. 

I also found the constant interruptions, the slow type speed of the conversations to be obnoxiously aggravating. The "assistant" rarely says anything of actual worth, and when taking data chunks in mid-conversation I really wish I could have switched him off, or the developers had limited his appearence. I also found the way that all new or unread data pinged up and highlighted in red meant that I almost never needed to think. I am sure that you could complete this game in a foriegn language just by clicking where the game told you, without understanding a single word of what's written. 

Now, having said all of this, I bought the game on sale and it's cheap. 5 hours of play time for £3.50- I guess there is a limit to what you can expect a studio to produce for that sort of budget. I'm pleased I didn't pay £7 for it though. 


Overall I think it's a poor handling of a great concept, and thus a wasted opportunity.

review_text_raw:
Short game with an interesting concept; that, in my opinion, failed to deliver. For the most part, the game does a good job keeping you guessing if you are making the right choices; but overall, I found the game boring and kept playing only to finish the story, just to be disappointed.

The entire gameplay loop consists of reading and dragging sentences from the right side of the screen to the left. Depending on your choices, the story can move in slightly different directions.

The story was interesting enough to keep me playing. You are an investigator working for a government surveillance system trying to unravel a terrorist group. The game wants you to deal with all the moral struggle that comes with invading people's privacy, but I think the premise falls flat. There were many times throughout the game where I felt it was finally about to get good, but it never materialized. Then the last chapter throws everything overboard: [spoiler] the criminal out themselves undermining all the mystery; the game tries to guilt you into feeling bad for people who had done terrible things; and, for some reason, you are supposed to side with them in the end. [/spoiler]

Too many conflicted opinions to recommend this one. I believe there is a Demo; try it first.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]: 
By the end of the game, there are dozens of pages of fictitious files and documents to sift through... and the game did NOT make that task much easier. Could I get some bookmarks, please?

[*][b][u]RAILROADING[/u][/b]: 
So, I won’t say much here out of respect for spoilers, but suffice it to say that the design choices made in the game make it very clear how the developers feel regarding the subject matter. This bias in design limited the scope of user choice and the kinds of endings you can get. It would have been very interesting to have a greater variety of outcomes. It would have also worked to underscore the sense of user agency that they’d worked so hard to create in the first place.

[*][b][u]Short Length [/u][/b]: 
I’ve finished 2 complete playthroughs at 11 hours... which, given the minimalism of the graphics, seems extremely short and makes the current price of $9.99 a bit pricey.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall a very interesting and unique experience that I mostly enjoyed. However, because of the political nature of the game and the railroading embedded by the developers, I don’t think I’ll be buying any DLC any time soon, nor would I recommend the game at its current price of $9.99.

review_text_raw: Orwell fails on a lot of levels. A lot of very fundamental writing levels. First and foremost it gives you a set of tools that allow you to see what people do on the internet and tasks you with finding the perpetrator of a bombing. You're given one prime suspect and as you progress your web of people of interest grows and grows. The principle gameplay mechanic involves choosing which specific pieces of information you choose to report to your orwellian system. Which will change how the game plays out. The first failure comes that it is often very obvious what information is going to affect what, as it is all highlighted in blue, or yellow if it conflicts with another piece of information. This is another problem. The conflict system makes very little sense most of the time. One of the first examples of the system in use involves a personal blog ran by a Person of Interest and an editorial they wrote for a newspaper. They both detail the same concept but with completely differeing opinions on the matter, and these pieces of information are considered a conflict and therefore cannot both be reported. While this specific instance makes very little gameplay difference either way it still makes no sense. Being able to report both pieces of information would have shown (at least to me) his willingness to play whatever side of an issue would get him paid, and could've sowed him as a much stronger suspect later on. Instead you have instances where you handler is confused by information you weren't able to provide them due to it being a conflict, when both pieces of information were true. This creates a very frustrating experience in trying to influence the story and with trying to keep information that is relevant to the story seperate from information that isnt. Another fundamental failing of the story telling is its ending, which if I'm perfectly honest; is godawful. To my knowledge, your choices throughout the game have no impact on the ending. There's just three buttons at the end. Push one for your ending. None of them making  a bit of sense. Right before your ending the perpetrator of the bombings reveals themselves, showing that the previous three chapters had all just been misdirection to make sure no player could possibly guess the real one and they basically say to you the player "And this is why your system doesn't work! You couldn't even figure out I was the perpetrator" When it was the game mechanics and information that was provided to you by the game that made it impossible to determine the perpetrator. They then ask you to take down the system, since you can now see it doesnt work. your other two options are to get a politician associated with your orwell system arrested, or to claim the group the perpetrator belongs to are all terrorists using out of context IMs. If you're thinking that this seems to be lacking a very obvious fourth option then I agree. My first instinct was simply to use the perpetrator admitting to instigating the bombings to get her arrested. As that would make sense, she admitted it to our face and yet there's no option present. Just the three arbitrary ones presented. In the end it was three chapters of intriguing build up for one chapter of letdowns and unguessable twists that completely kill the narrative, suspension of disbelief, and immersion. 4/10

review_text_raw:
The story is good (although there are some dumb plot twists), but gameplay is almost non-existent: the game is all about reading and dragging marked chunks of text to a profile of corresponding person. This requires zero thought and deduction.

Overall, Orwell feels like a more boring version of Papers, Please. Despite the fact some of your decisions influense the outcome, the game feels like a chore.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What Orwell is?

In Orwell, you are the operator of the super software that can trace every citizen digital information, and you are after  a terrorism activist group called Thought who plans to disrupt society safety through violent manifests. Then reason behind it is fear for government peeping your personal life a la NSA/Edward Snowden case. 

My thoughts

The Detective Hacking game mode made me to instant purchase Orwell game, as it combines two of my favorites genres. However it turned out to be VERY frustrating to me.

Slow pacing: I did not expect this game to be in pace with some freaky japanese action game, however what I felt is that they tried to compensate this short game with a slow pace of events combined with tons of wall texts for you to read, search, and try to link pieces with terrorisms acts. You will spend a lot of minutes reading dialogues, text messages, emails, even facebook posts lol, and others stuff, to figure out who is who, and where to go next.

Story: It has only one mainplot, no additional stages or cases, which made me judge the worthness of this purchase. The plot is short, and again, what made it last 9 hours are a bunch of useless information that visually polluted the game, and contributed barely nothing to the storyline. You spend most of your time digging useless information that sometimes take you to nowhere and suprisingly to the next part. One example, how the US gov do not even know a US citizen full name, dob, place of work? Any normal citizen could just Google them to figure out, however you find yourself stuck into finding this information no matter what! (lol) In the beginning there was some air of suspense about some terrorism acts suspects, however at the end... it was pretty lame the way it turned out. And what is even sadder is that in the end you are not in control of how the game ends, so choices don't really matter. After finishing Orwell, you can only describe this game as a Visual Novel game, and not a Detective Hacking game.

Some small rantings regarding the storyline

Spoiler 1:  [spoiler] You are the US government and you can't access a blocked article in a blog lul. [/spoiler]

Spoiler 2:  [spoiler] You are the US government and has one of super softwares but can't even trace where the suspects are [/spoiler]

Spoiler 3:  [spoiler] How the fuck some small time hacker could crack into US government super secret software so easily? Let's hope China, N. Korea, Russia, or any other terrorism groups do not hire him! [/spoiler]


Price: It expensive to pay USD 10.00 for a game with 9 hours duration, and has ZERO replayability value. Just compare it to Stardew Valley which full price is USD 15.00, now USD 10.00 in Steam Autumn Sales, which I have played over 120 hours, and has even more hundreds of gameplay and replay...

In my opinion Orwell has a cool innovative gameplay, however only one plot with useless amount of background stories to make it last longer than it should, with zero suspense effect at the end. And the only thing that you expect in this kind of game, is having to work on several complex different cases, which did not happen. Also choices did not matter in the end.

If you still don't care and want to purchase Orwell, my advice would be to wait for the Christmas sale or price drop. Peace & GG.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Unfortunately I didn't enjoy Orwell at all. Admittedly, it's been a sponatenous purchase, done out of sheer curiosity to see what the fuzz is all about.

But instead of a dystopian thriller, blending story and gameplay together with an innovative user interface, I got quite a dull experience.

Actually Orwell isn't a game at all, it's rather a semi-interactive story which simply progresses together with the text snippets you highlight  ("upload"). To make things a bit more interesting, your fictional self is supposed to participate in a surveillance and data mining program which observes persons and evaluates their behavior. You do that by browsing through social media profiles, reading blogs, newspapers, looking at photos and following text chats.

Noticed something? Yes, it's basically down to reading. The whole game could have been perfectly realized via a website, there is basically only a minimal amount of graphic assets involved. Now while that might work out for a well written game, it unfortunately fails for Orwell.

The story line tries to explore the important question of privacy, civil liberties and how social media and data mining can lead to their erosion, especially in light of an ubiqitous fear of terrorist acts.

But whoever wrote Orwell did it so heavy-handedly, that you quickly feel like you're stuck in a school lesson, with the teacher dancing around the obvious answer, because he thinks it's too complicated for you to understand it right away.

Even worse, while you might even find the person you follow being an interesting character, making you feel invested in how your actions will affect their life, you are constantly delayed by the process of gathering key information which will trigger the next story snippet.

And no, it's not interesting to browse through some fictional website, filled with trite and shallow pseudo-philosophical ramblings, in order to find that little piece of incriminating information which will suddenly prompt your supervisor to announce the next story progress ("she's a suspect, let's wiretap her / she's guilty, I am sending in the force with an arrest warrant). 

Actually it's quickly making you search for the next key snippet, dragging it to the upload window, just to rinse and repeat with another source you'll be presented with.

So bottom line, while playing Orwell I wondered what I am actually doing here.

If I want to have a linear story, presented (mainly) via text, guess what? Yes, I'll read a book. The benefit of doing so is that it's very probably better written, more accessible and I don't need to stare at a screen.

If I want to play a game, I will play a game. But then I expect something to actually utilize the manifold ways of presenting a story and of including me, the player (not reader), in its progress. (And yes, I actually play some classic text-adventure now and then.)

Orwell is neither the first nor the latter. It's an experiment which seems to aim high, but soon falls flat in its core design. After an hour I had enough. I'm not feeling invested or intrigued to continue at all, so Orwell will join the forbidden crypt of mistakes somewhere in the forsaken depths of my library.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is one of the few I don’t really feel I can fall down on either side. Ultimately, I felt I should mark it as unrecommended because I couldn’t bring myself to give it a thumbs up, and steam doesn’t have a ‘meh, its ok I guess’ option.

The story is, literally as it is titled, an Orwellian style, drama, I guess. Unfortunately the railroading detracts from the telling. 

The game play is actually pretty good and quite well done. As an investigator you’re expected to dig up as much information as you can regarding suspects in a terrorist attack, and then use their connections and the information gleaned to unpick what occurred and who is responsible, with the ultimate aim of preventing another attack. It is actually the limitations that are forced upon you to ensure you don’t get lost, combined with the multitude of ‘coincidences’ and other sloppy writing that only drives the story in a railroaded direction that bring the whole thing down.

Pros:
The game is easy to play, for the most part allows you to take your time reading the information and make your decision. The way the information is presented is also easy to digest and use. 
The characters are each unique and seem quite well thought out with their own motivations and histories. They also have an interesting dynamic that shows the growth, depth, and fading of their friendship as natural friendships have done.


Cons: 
The game opens with a single character to investigate, while that makes sense from a tutorial point, it doesn’t from a story point. This then focus and railroading leading to a contrived conclusion full of plot holes and excuses kinda ruins the game.
The system showcases a really interesting idea for ways to gather and profile information, monitor suspects, and use what you learn to further an investigation. Then it doesn’t let you do it, restricting what you can see to only a tiny window. It makes for a surveillance system that can’t watch anything.
Tying in to the above, we have so much information on the characters, but can’t utilise any of the information we would undoubtedly be able to access as law enforcement. Once again it felt like an artificial restriction, which was most frustrating.

Suggested improvements:
A skip dialogue button. Most of the few hours I’ve racked up were waiting for conversations to end.
Allow the system to access some of the surveyed individual’s data and build the puzzle environment that way.
Allow us to use the system in the ways we feel fit, not just the way that gives the narrative held.
For the love of god, let us investigate more people, more red herrings. Let us be the ones to cross off people from the lists, let us be the ones that decide what’s worth pursuing. 

Overall Recommendation:
This game has so much potential as a story driven and person centred hook. Especially for people who enjoy info hunts or detective style games. I can see it being really expandable with so many story options.
I think if you like that kind of game, this will scratch an itch for you.
But I can’t recommend it in its current state. As it is it comes off negatively and that just spoils all of the good things about it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TL;DR: If you want to be a pedantic bureaucrat, play "Papers, please" instead.


Long story:

This can be an exciting game if you're not one who likes nitpicking. However, if you do (which is maybe why you're drawn to it in the first place), you will pull some hairs out in rage and discontent.

The game focuses on monitoring an increasing set of data (news, websites, chat logs, phone calls etc) to look for leads in a specific case on which the game is built up. Whatever the game means is relevant will be highlighted, and you'll have the choice to either submit it to the investigators or ignore it. The info will also be rewritten, i.e. concentrated to what the game thinks it means.

This poses two problems - 1) the data YOU might think is highly relevant or more relevant isn't highlighted. And 2) the data you find may not be the data that will be submitted. For example, someone SUGGESTS to someone else that they do something. If you submit it, it's altered to say that the person PLANNED it. When talking about a crime that may or may not have occurred, this is a very important difference. Casually suggesting something and planning it is not the same. Everything you submit will be used by the police to decide which actions to take, so you might want to ignore that piece of info then.. if you can (explained further down).

Sometimes you find "contradicting info", and you can only pick one of the contradicting pieces (or ignore them altogether, of course). Sometimes these pieces of information don't contradict each other, but you still have to pick only one.

The game follows a story, and some key facts are needed in order to move it along. Once in a while you experience that the game doesn't progress, apparently because it won't continue until you've provided a key "fact" in the story. So you'll have to go through the stuff you ignored and guess which one the game wants you to submit before moving on. And yes, sometimes that includes incorrect information. Which causes rage quitting on my part, because the whole point of you making sure facts are provided is taken away.

The developers should have points for making a complex story and managing to implement this as a game - the way they have made it both simple, complex and engaging should be praised, as well as the psychological profiles of the suspects, showing how easily having inner access to their thoughts without having the proper context can lead to false conclusions. But the lack of preciseness and logical snafus in the interface makes what could have been an interesting take at the pros and cons of the surveillance society into a silly, semi-intellectual murder mystery for the masses.

review_text_raw:
Given all the positive reviews, I thought Orwell would be a more interesting game than it actually is.
But the gameplay is mostly boring. In a way, it is very similar to a text-adventure game. You read through/listen to all the documents given access to (webpages, chat sessions or phone calls). But there is basically no investigative work, hacking or anything that would be fun to do to find information. All the work is already done for you, every document is already analyzed, and you cannot investigate new people before being allowed to, even if it is clear they must have some role in the investigation.

So yes, the gameplay is overly simple and very linear, but maybe I could have been ok with it if I had found the story interesting.
But the story is boring. The main goal in the game (at least until I stopped playing) is to find the culprits responsible for a bomb attack. Sounds exciting right? Except most of the info you have to read through is about the different suspects boring life, relationships and habits, things I don't give a damn about. So I guess this game is not for me.

Maybe the game becomes more complex and interesting later on (I really hope so), but I am just not interested enough so far in the story to continue playing. Maybe I'll try again later...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't ever write reviews, but I have an overwhelming urge to say what's on my mind. With no one to rant to, I'll just use this as an outlet (and it'll provide good reference material when i come back in a couple years to figure out why i didn't like this game).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Gameplay / Mechanics[/b]

the game is simple. you parse information for the important bits and then drag and drop that information into people's profiles. the game pre-selects certain segments of text and highlights them for you and then gives you the choice of determining whether it's important or true enough to include in their file. and therein lies the problem. you're given almost no autonomy, making the game less engaging. 99% of the time, you just scroll through articles and web pages looking for the highlighted text and then dragging and dropping it. there's no limit to how much data i can gather, so i don't have to think about whether this information is important enough to include and just include it anyway. and any false information that might be misleading is made extremely obvious. like when someone lists their address as "the interwebs". if there's any data that conflicts with another piece of data, it's highlighted in yellow and presented to you as a choice. you can only choose one of these to include in their file and your decision will effect the outcome (or so i assume, having not played the game more than once). these are the more engaging parts of the game as it forces me to analyze both data chunks' context and make a real decision. but each of these moments are fleeting and within a handful of seconds, i'm back to mindlessly scrolling through files again. there's one moment in the game that breaks this trend. they limit the amount of information you can include and that was the best part of the game. i actually had to sit down and read everything before figuring out what parts i thought were important. for the first time, i actually felt immersed in this world and my role in it. that's how i think the whole game should have been. instead, i was given brainless and mundane tasks, leaving me twiddling my thumbs for the majority of the game.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Story[/b]

the story is actually pretty good. the mystery is slowly unraveled as you discover more information and you're given a few twists and turns to keep you on your toes. the story is paced well, nothing feels rushed or pedantically slow and takes its own time to develop its characters and world. the characters feel real. a couple fall to mere caricatures, but the game does well at representing these characters in more than one dimension. take for example nina, a character who at first seems like an extremist but is slowly revealed to be a single mother just trying to make ends meet by doing odd jobs. the only character that irritated me was your supervisor. every time you select a piece of information, he [i]has to[/i] comment on it in some way. he either made comments that don't matter and just made me roll my eyes (like when one character said they didn't like the government and your supervisor [i]just had to say[/i] "we don't like you either"). or he recapped [i]exactly[/i] what that data chunk said. or he told you something that was already extremely obvious (like when you find out that goldfels is already dead, he says "that means he couldn't be behind the bombings and someone is impersonating him". no duh). so when he gets targeted, i don't feel a whole lot of sympathy for him. 

i do not, however, like how the story is presented. the game consciously trades its gameplay for its narrative. you start to feel like less of an investigator trying to solve a mystery and more like a disneyland park goer on the [i]it's a a small world[/i] ride. you take a backseat and just watch what happens. contrast this to [i]Firewatch[/i], a similarly narrative driven game. it's mechanics are also extremely basic and boils down to a walking simulator game, but it delivers its story masterfully and makes you feel like [i]you[/i] are uncovering everything instead of everything being spat at you (like orwell does).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Main Message[/b]

the game's main focus is to postulate the question, "should you trade privacy for security?" to which it answers "no". you take the role of what is essentially the thought police from george orwell's [i]1984[/i] and the game attempts to show you the inherent flaw of this. the end of the game breaks the fourth wall and speaks to you directly, asking you if what you've been doing is really okay. if spying on people is ethical or not, then puts the power in your hands. you can either expose the people you've been spying on this whole time or expose your boss. the problem is, the game never once makes me feel guilty or wrong or disgusted for having spied on these people's lives. in fact, it actively makes us feel justified for it. i stopped a bomb from going off in the biggest mall in the city. and when it came time to make that big decision in the end, of course i chose to expose this "thought" group because they rigged bombs and killed innocents. the game never addresses the morality of all of this and never makes me feel like i've overstepped my boundaries and question my actions. 

imagine this, as i'm going through a suspect's files (bob), i stumble upon bank statements that shows regular large-sum withdrawals. in some private conversations with his wife, he mentions having to take business trips, but his company's official records never mention any. we discover that he has a second phone with which he only contacts one person. the whole thing seems really shady and we have text messages of them planning to meet at the plaza an hour before the explosion, mentioning that he'll bring "the money". we get word that there's going to be another bombing within the hour. with the pressure mounting, we send in the police to intervene in the bob's next meeting and arrest them. during the interrogation, the bomb goes off. we find out that the bob's relation to his "contact" is a woman with which he had a one night fling and together had a baby, despite already having a family. they've been meeting together secretly so he can act as a stand-in father and support the them financially. bob loves his wife and kids and recognizes that he made a big mistake and is just trying to do his best in this crazy world. he has a responsibility to both his wife and his "contact". then sometime later (perhaps a couple chapters) we read a news article that says bob killed himself, detailing the events of his affair and how his wife divorced him. imagine how gut-wrenching that would be. to know that we ruined a guy's life because of what we did. by the end of the game, when we're asked whether or not what we did was right, that thought would would weigh heavy on my mind.

the game ends with an exposition based on your choices. in my case, the thought group is arrested and orwell is seeing full funding and support. it then has us start a profile on our own character like we've been doing all game, showing that we're also being spied on without our notice. i feel like this was supposed to be a punch to the gut, an immediate eye-opener, but it didn't do much for me. it would've been a lot more effective if it could pull information from my OS or my steam account and fill in the blanks with my real name, date of birth, email, etc. that would feel creepy and make my skin crawl a bit.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Orwell was a missed opportunity. it had a lot of potential to address contemporary issues with the ever-real presence of a "big brother" type figure spying on us even now. but the game falls flat and fails to gain my sympathy. the game feels like it was written by a 16 year old who just read [i]1984[/i] and circle-jerks how "deep" it is.

It's disappointing because it could have been so much more.

When I was playing it though the structure of the game felt off to me, there was too little freedom to discover for myself the conspiracy that was going on. Certain necessary options are highlighted beforehand, so that skimming (or even skipping) the text was an option. Any puzzle/detective game that is as on-rails as this one is bound to lack any critical reasoning.

Also the use of Orwellian politics is so reductive that it almost entirely avoids any real political discussion (bad State controls people, we need "freedom", whatever that is).

My advice is that if you want political commentary then read a book instead. If you want a good detective story then read a book instead. Either way I'd rather read a book than play this game any day,

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Running on PopOS Linux (and this game has a linux client)... crashed on activating the first achievement.

Which is about the time I was ready to walk away from the game anyway.

Interesting idea, and definitely innovative as far as visual novels go, but that's all this is... another visual novel masquerading as an adventure game. You don't have to play hours and hours of this to figure out that your choices might provide some slight deviations in the story, but ultimately it's a very narrow path.

There is no adventure here, there are no puzzles.

The interactivity involves dragging across auto-highlighted data you "discover" to build a profile, as well as other profiles connecting to your primary suspect... all from static articles/reports/etc. and active chat sessions that you monitor. No reading through and figuring out what data has actual value the way it is done in the real world. You can read it all, but that isn't really necessary... just skim and speed click your way ahead and you can push the story forward. Feel like you're stuck, something that hasn't been done will remain "starred", so you can go back to that article or whatever and the game will what to do.

Policing/Defense/Military/Whatever-Agency surveillance staff that perform these profile building intelligence jobs and put together these profiles... it's an interesting concept that could have been turned into a fascinating text heavy game that required minimal computing resources or HDD footprint... but the NPC that is effectively your handler guides you the whole way, further holding your hand on top of the highlighted text/data that tells you that you can do something.

That completely kills any mental engagement on a gaming level. You are simply a consumer of a story, which is fine... but that's not a game. That's an interactive short story, or an animated slide show/film/something... not a game.

Steam needs to enforce some sort of standard for the tags to many of these types of "games"... your choices don't really matter here. And a politically themed visual novel that constantly tells you and shows you what to do... that does not qualify as being a "sim". You do not need to "think" when you play Orwell, just obey orders and click where you are allowed to click... you could almost mistake it for a poetic and poignant Orwellian statement on its own existence as a "game"...  but it's not. It really is not.

review_text_raw:
Orwell is one of those games I played several years ago, that still elicits a groan of disgust everytime I see it in my games library. 

The game concept itself sounds extremely interesting and intriguing, but the game itself doesn't care as much about the game mechanics as it does the uninteresting writing about its unlikeable cast. All of the characters I quickly grew to dislike as I felt they were caricatures of what an amateur creative writer thought 'interesting' people would act like. I dislike the geometric art style and feel it feels particularly dated (though I've never liked it), but that's more of a personal taste.

The first act was the strongest as I hadn't grown tired of the writing yet, and the plot hadn't started indulging in it's pointless conspiracy drivel that dominates the later acts. The writing wears its politics on its sleeves with the implicit assumption that the player shares the authors values which even if you do will feel grating. 

The ending and climax are the worst offenders because what should feel like a reward for finishing the game just felt unrewarding and absurd. It eschews all world-building and you have to accept the conceit that there's only like 20 people in its world. Consequences are divorced from logic and it feels terrible. Granted I know there are multiple endings, however to reach another one I would have to play through this terrible game again, and it's simply, completely not worth it. 

I recommend avoid.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Is this really a game. Seems more like an interactive movie than a game. I don't think there is any way to win or lose in this "game" and more of just someone who is trying to spread their own agenda I guess. Seems kinda ironic given the nature of the "game" itself. It's basically the storyline taken from the Snowden incident. It did keep me entertained for a few hours, but when you have nothing else to do, it's not very difficult. Wouldn't recommend buying this, but if you get it for free, it's worth messing around with it when you get bored of everything else.
